extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and researchers preparing notes and bibliographies for academic or professional publications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming citations and bibliographic entries for a wide range of special source types (classical works, inscriptions, musical scores, databases, patents, audiovisual media, legal documents, etc.). Focuses on which elements to include, typographic treatment, order, and short-form/online conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superscripts in classical references
rubrics_metrics.description: In classical references, a superior figure is sometimes used immediately after the title of a work (or its abbreviation), and preceding any other punctuation, to indicate the number of the edition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use superscripted edition numbers immediately after titles/abbreviations and before punctuation when following classical-reference practice. Examples provided (e.g., Stolz-Schmalz, Lat. Gram. (rev. Leumann-Hoffmann; Munich, 1928), 390-91).

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters with numerals in classical citations
rubrics_metrics.description: In former practice, the letters accompanying numerals in citations of classical works sometimes appeared as superscripts (e.g., 3.2.9965-8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that older practice may show letters as superscripts; modern practice generally follows the conventions laid out elsewhere in the section (see 14.243).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collections of inscriptions — numbering and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arabic numerals are used in references to volumes in collections of inscriptions. Periods follow the volume and inscription numbers, and further subdivisions are treated as in other classical references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format examples: IG 22,3274. or IG Rom. 3.739.9-10. Use periods to separate volume/inscription/subdivisions and follow general classical reference subdivision rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collections cited by editor's name
rubrics_metrics.description: Some collections are cited only by the name of the editor. Since the editor’s name here stands in place of a title, no comma is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Dessau 6964.23-29. Treat the editor name as the title element and omit a comma between editor name and subsequent locators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fragments of classical texts — numbering and editor attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Fragments are not uniformly numbered; numbering is usually unique to a particular edition. Two numbers separated by a period usually indicate fragment and line. The editor’s name must follow the number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite as: Empedocles, frag. 115 Diels-Kranz. For multiple editions of same fragments, use parentheses or an equals sign to show correspondence (e.g., frag. 133 Bergk (frag. 127 Bowra) or frag. 133 Bergk = 127 Bowra).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern editions of classics — page citations require edition
rubrics_metrics.description: When Greek, Latin, or medieval classics are cited by page number, the edition must be specified, and the normal rules for citing books are followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always name the edition/editor when giving page numbers (e.g., Propertius, Elegies, ed. and trans. G. P. Goold, Loeb Classical Library 18 (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1990), 45).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply classical reference form to medieval works
rubrics_metrics.description: The form for classical references may equally well be applied to medieval works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may cite medieval works using the same conventions as classical references; include edition/translation details when necessary. Examples given (e.g., Augustine, De civitate Dei 20.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing classic English poems and plays — divisions and omission of publication facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Classic English poems and plays can often be cited by book, canto, and stanza; stanza and line; act, scene, and line; or similar divisions. Publication facts can then be omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For frequently cited works (especially Shakespeare), normally specify the edition in the first note or in the bibliography; edition must be mentioned if page numbers are cited. Examples: Chaucer, 'Wife of Bath’s Prologue,' Canterbury Tales, frag. 3, lines 105-14.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short forms for classic English poems and plays
rubrics_metrics.description: A citation may be shortened by omitting act, line, and the like, as long as the system used has been explained. Arabic numerals are used, separated by periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In immediately succeeding references, it is usually safer to repeat all the numbers. The author’s name may be omitted if clear from the text. For sources in text see 13.67. Examples: Pope, Rape of the Lock, 3.28-29.

rubrics_metrics.name: Published musical scores treated like books
rubrics_metrics.description: Published musical scores are treated in much the same way as books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include title, librettist/composer as appropriate, editor, volume/series info, publisher, and date. Example provided: Giuseppe Verdi, Il corsaro..., ed. Elizabeth Hudson, 2 vols., The Works of Giuseppe Verdi, ser. 1, Operas (Chicago: University of Chicago Press; Milan: G. Ricordi, 1998).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpublished scores treated as manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Unpublished scores are treated in the same way as other unpublished material in manuscript collections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow manuscript-collection citation rules (see 14.221-31). Example: Ralph Shapey, 'Partita for Violin and Thirteen Players,' score, 1966, Special Collections, Joseph Regenstein Library, University of Chicago.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing scientific databases — minimum elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite data from a database by listing at a minimum: the name of the database, a descriptive phrase or record locator indicating the part of the database being cited, an access date, and a URL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bibliographies, list under the name of the database. Examples: NASA/IPAC Extragalactic Database (object name ...; accessed April 6, 2016), http://...; GenBank (for RP11-... [accession number ...]; accessed April 6, 2016), http://...

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents — citation elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are cited under the names of the creators and dated by the year of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include inventor names, title (if applicable), patent number, filing date, and issue date. Example: Iizuka, Masanori, and Hideki Tanaka. Cement admixture. US Patent 4,586,960, filed June 26, 1984, and issued May 6, 1986.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards — citation elements and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: To cite a standard published by an industry group or standards organization, include the name of the organization, the title of the standard (in italics), an edition or other identifying number or label, and publication information. Online standards should include a URL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In notes, standards can be cited by title; in a bibliography entry, list under the group or organization even if that entity is also the publisher. Examples provided (ANSI/NISO, W3C XML).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citations taken from secondary sources — discourage and required format
rubrics_metrics.description: To cite a source from a secondary source ('quoted in . . .') is generally to be discouraged; if an original source is unavailable, both the original and the secondary source must be listed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the original citation and indicate it was quoted in the secondary source (example: Louis Zukofsky ... quoted in Bonnie Costello, Marianne Moore: Imaginary Possessions...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia citation elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The citation for recordings and other multimedia content usually includes some or all of these elements: (1) primary responsible person; (2) title; (3) information about the work (contributors, date, location); (4) publisher information; (5) medium/format; (6) supplementary info (number of discs, duration); (7) URL for online sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order and inclusion of elements depend on the nature of the source and whether a part or whole is cited and who is the focus of the citation. See 8.197 for typographic treatment of titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discographies and filmographies — presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Discographies, filmographies, and the like are specialized bibliographies that list (and sometimes annotate) audiovisual materials; they are modeled on notes and bibliography entries but may be presented as a separate list or appendix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place such lists preceding the bibliography or as an appendix (see 14.63) and consult specialized bibliographic advice where relevant (e.g., Suzanne E. Thorin for music). See figure 14.12 for an example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical recordings — who to list first and date conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: List by author, performer, or other primary contributor; if conductor or performer is the focus, list them first. For the date include recording, copyright, or published date; if unknown use 'n.d.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If missing metadata (common with older recordings or downloads), consult library catalogs; citations without such information are generally unacceptable. Acquisition numbers follow publisher with no intervening comma. For streaming, list the service or file format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group musical recordings in discography rather than bibliography
rubrics_metrics.description: Musical recordings are usually listed in a separate discography rather than in a bibliography. If included in a bibliography, group them under an appropriate subhead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See fig. 14.12 and 14.262 for layout examples and suggested grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recorded readings, lectures, audiobooks — treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Recordings of drama, prose or poetry readings, lectures, and the like are treated much the same as musical recordings; publication facts follow print-media style where needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include performer, title, publisher/label, date, physical or digital format, duration, and URL if online. Examples include Dylan Thomas under Milk Wood entries and presidential speeches hosted by archives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video and film recordings — citation variability and indexed scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations of video and film recordings will vary according to nature (television show, movie, etc.). Any facts relevant to identifying the item should be included. Indexed scenes are treated as chapters and cited by title or number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include director, episode title, writers, principal performers, air/release date, distributor/media format, and URL if applicable. When citing material original to a later edition, cite the edition being used and omit original release date where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live performances — usually sufficient in text/notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Live performances cannot be consulted as such by readers; it is generally sufficient to mention details in the text or notes rather than in a bibliography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include name/location of venue and date, and any information needed to identify the performance per the multimedia guidelines (14.261). If citing a recording of the live performance, consult recording examples (14.263–14.265).

rubrics_metrics.name: Online multimedia and apps — URL and access-date practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite online multimedia according to the multimedia recommendations and include a URL as the final element. If no date can be determined, include the access date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the material is a recording of a speech or a digital version of a published source, include information about the original performance or source. Exercise caution citing copies posted without publisher/sponsor ties. For browser-run multimedia, file format needn't be mentioned; for downloadable files specify the format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia app content — version and device info
rubrics_metrics.description: To cite multimedia apps include any version number and information about the device or operating system required to run the app.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also include publishing information adapted from the recorded/multimedia citation conventions (example: Gems and Jewels, iPad ed., v. 1.01 (Touchpress, 2011); Angry Birds Transformers, v. 1.4.25 (Rovio Entertainment, 2014), Android 4.0 or later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended stylebooks for legal citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations in predominantly legal works generally follow one of two guides: The Bluebook or the ALWD Guide to Legal Citation. Chicago recommends using one of these systems for legal and public documents even in nonlegal works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors working extensively with legal/public documents should have one of these manuals on hand. The section's examples are mostly based on The Bluebook, with exceptions noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/public documents online — preference and authentication
rubrics_metrics.description: For cases, constitutions, statutes, and similar materials, print sources are preferred, but online versions authenticated by a government entity or considered the official version can be treated as print. A URL may be appended as the last element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For commercial databases include database name and id (or currency info for statutes/constitutions). For nonlegal sources consulted online, follow Chicago's general online recommendations (14.6–18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Note form for legal-style citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal publications use notes for documentation and rarely include bibliographies. Any work so cited need not be listed in a bibliography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works using the author-date style that cite only a handful of legal/public documents may limit those citations to the text; those with more than a very few legal-style citations may need to supplement author-date with footnotes or endnotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typefaces in legal-style citations
rubrics_metrics.description: In Bluebook style, italics are used for titles of articles and chapters, uncommon foreign words or phrases (but not well-known terms like de facto), certain introductory signals, case history, and procedural phrases. Case names in textual sentences are italicized; all other material appears in roman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bluebook also specifies caps and small caps for constitutions, titles, and authors; the examples in this section use a simpler style (upper- and lowercase roman) in some places. Consult The Bluebook for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page numbers and locators in legal-style citations
rubrics_metrics.description: For most sources the first page number is cited (the opening page); references to specific page numbers follow the first page number, separated by a comma. Some sources are cited by section (§) or paragraph (¶) number; references to specific pages within such sections follow a comma and at (in roman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'at' to cite a particular page in shortened citations. Examples demonstrate '222 F.3d 141, 145' and '222 F.3d at 145.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations in legal-style citations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bluebook specifies abbreviations for reporters, cases, courts, legislative documents, journals, and compilation services, and guidelines for certain shortened terms. Most Bluebook abbreviations use periods or apostrophes, with exceptions for organization initialisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bluebook uses '2d' and '3d' rather than '2nd' and '3rd' for ordinals in citations and capitalizes abbreviations like 'No.' and 'Sess.' Differences from Chicago exist and should be handled per the chosen manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short forms in legal citations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bluebook allows certain short forms for subsequent citations (e.g., case names reduced to one party, statutes identified by name and section, use of id.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short forms are common for cases; works with very few legal citations may prefer to use full forms for clarity. Note use limitations in electronic contexts (see id. warning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cases and court decisions — basic citation elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Full case names in citations, including the abbreviation v., are set in roman in notes; short forms in subsequent citations are italicized. Full citations include volume number (arabic), abbreviated reporter name, series ordinal (if applicable), abbreviated court name (if not indicated by the reporter) and the date in parentheses, and other relevant info.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single page designates the opening page of a decision; an additional number designates an actual page cited. Use 'at' in shortened citations to indicate a particular page. Examples: United States v. Christmas, 222 F.3d 141, 145 (4th Cir. 2000); Christmas, 222 F.3d at 145.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cases consulted online and commercial databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases consulted online should normally be cited to the appropriate reporter(s). A URL that points directly to an official resource may be appended. When citing commercial electronic databases, include the docket number, database name, and any identifying date and number supplied; references to page/screen numbers are preceded by an asterisk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short forms for database-cited cases may include only the database identifier. Examples: Family Serv. Ass’n v. Wells Twp., No. 14-4020, 2015 U.S. App. LEXIS 6174 (6th Cir. Apr. 16, 2015).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme, federal, and state court citation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme Court decisions are preferably cited to United States Reports (U.S.); lower federal-court decisions to Federal Reporter or Federal Supplement; state/local decisions much like federal. Court name often indicated by reporter and need not be repeated. Include case history where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to reporter abbreviations, series ordinals, and spacing conventions (e.g., 'Cal. 2d' has a space; initialisms like 'A.2d' do not). Use examples provided to format citations correctly (Citizens United v. FEC, 558 U.S. 310 (2010); Williams v. Davis, 27 Cal. 2d 746 (1946)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding id. in electronic formats
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is important to avoid id. (as in an electronic format where individual notes may be presented out of context), use a shortened citation form instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a shortened citation that is still unambiguous (e.g., 'Williams, 27 Cal. 2d at 747').

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutions — numerals and capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In citations to constitutions, the article and amendment numbers appear in roman numerals; other subdivision numbers are in arabic. In Bluebook style the name of the constitution is capitalized; other abbreviations are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: U.S. Const. art. I, § 4, cl. 2; U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 2. For nonlegal style see 9.28.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative and executive documents — abbreviations and omission rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations for federal legislative documents include 'Cong.' (Congress), 'H.' (House), 'S.' (Senate). Unless not clear from context, 'U.S.' may be omitted. For House and Senate documents published as of 1907, the session number can generally be omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult The Bluebook for lists of abbreviations and many examples. Examples show how to cite bills, resolutions, statutes, and session laws (e.g., Safe and Accurate Food Labeling Act of 2015, H.R. 1599, 114th Cong. (2015)).
